title: Shadow deployment
story:
A shadow deployment runs the new thing on real traffic and throws its output away. Users see the existing system and only the existing system; the new one answers the same questions beside it, silently, and everything it produces goes into storage rather than to anybody. For the price of some compute you get the one thing no test set can give you: the real distribution of what people actually ask, at real volume, including the inputs nobody would have thought to write down.

That last part is most of the value. Your case set contains the questions you imagined and the failures you already found. Real traffic contains the malformed, the ambiguous, the extremely long, the ones in another language, the ones that are not questions at all, and the ones that are about something you did not know your system was being used for. A new component that looks excellent on the set can fall over on the real mixture, and shadow running is how you find that out with nobody watching.

It answers a specific list of questions well. Does it work on the actual distribution rather than the imagined one. Is it fast enough under real concurrency. Does it cost what the estimate said. What fraction of inputs does it fail on, and are those failures a category or a scatter. Where does it disagree with the current system, and on what kind of question.

And it cannot answer the one people most want it to. Whether users prefer it, or would use it more, or would trust it, is unanswerable from shadow traffic, because no user ever saw the output. Shadow measures the system; it does not measure the reception. Those need real exposure to a small number of people, and confusing the two is how something technically superior ships to an audience that hates it.

Now the thing that goes wrong, and it goes wrong often enough to state bluntly. A shadow that has side effects is not a shadow. If the shadow path can call a tool that sends a message, writes a record, charges a card or files a ticket, then it is a second production system operating without supervision, and you will find out when somebody receives two of something. Every tool on that path must be read-only, sandboxed or stubbed, and this needs checking rather than assuming, because the path usually reuses the same tool layer as production and the default is to work.

Run it off the request path. A shadow call made synchronously inside the real request doubles the latency the user waits for, which converts an experiment into an outage. Put the inputs on a queue, run the shadow asynchronously, and let it fall behind if it needs to — nobody is waiting for it, which is the entire point.

When you compare, compare disagreements rather than aggregates. The overall scores can be identical while one system is better on one category and worse on another, and that is the case you most need to see. Sample where they differ, have a person judge a few dozen, and sort the disagreements by kind. Which produces the second benefit of the whole exercise: those disagreements are exactly the cases worth adding to your evaluation set. A shadow deployment run for a week hands you a better case set as a side effect, drawn from real traffic and pre-filtered to the places where two reasonable systems do not agree.

problem.name: Testing on real traffic without exposure
problem.shape: A new component needs to meet the real distribution of inputs before any user depends on it.
tell: the new component performs well on the case set and has never seen real traffic
the shadow path shares the production tool layer and nobody has checked what it can call
the shadow call is made inside the user's request
results are compared as aggregate scores rather than by where the two systems disagree
problem.move: Mirror real inputs to the new component asynchronously off a queue, discard its output, ensure every tool on that path is read-only or stubbed, then compare by sampling disagreements and feed those cases into the evaluation set.
problem.invariant: The shadow output reaches nobody, so the experiment carries no user risk — which holds only while nothing on the shadow path has side effects.
problem.breaks: It cannot measure reception at all, because no user saw the output, so preference and trust still require exposing a small number of real people.

cost.time: every mirrored request is inference paid twice, for an experiment rather than a product
cost.space: shadow outputs have to be stored to be compared, which is the same storage discipline as reproducibility
cost.beats: a staged rollout, which measures reception and puts users at risk, and testing on the case set alone, which contains only inputs somebody imagined

problem.practice: Before mirroring anything, list every tool the new component can reach and mark each one read-only, sandboxed or stubbed. If you cannot complete that list quickly, you do not yet know what your shadow can do — and that, rather than the comparison, is the first thing the exercise has taught you.

beats.broke: A component is judged on a case set containing only inputs somebody imagined, so the real mixture — malformed, ambiguous, unexpected — is first met in production.
beats.fix: Mirror real traffic asynchronously to the new component, discard its output, and compare by sampling where it disagrees with the current system.
beats.cost: Inference is paid twice for an experiment, and the whole safety property depends on every tool in the shadow path being incapable of side effects.

interview.q: What does shadow running tell you that an evaluation set cannot, and what can it never tell you?
interview.trap: Assuming the shadow path is harmless. It usually reuses the production tool layer, so unless every tool is read-only, sandboxed or stubbed it is a second unsupervised production system.
interview.answer:
It gives me the real distribution at real volume — the malformed, ambiguous, very long, wrong-language, not-actually-a-question inputs, and the uses I did not know existed. My case set only holds what I imagined and what already failed, so something can look excellent there and fall over on the real mixture.

Concretely it answers whether it works on the actual distribution, whether it is fast enough under real concurrency, whether it costs what was estimated, what fraction of inputs it fails on and whether those failures form a category, and where it disagrees with the current system.

What it can never answer is reception — preference, trust, usage — because nobody saw the output. Shadow measures the system, not the reception, and confusing the two ships something technically better to an audience that dislikes it.

The operational care is side effects: if the shadow path can send, write, charge or file, it is a second production system running unsupervised, and I find out when someone gets two of something. So every tool on that path is read-only, sandboxed or stubbed, checked rather than assumed. And I run it off a queue, because a synchronous shadow call doubles the user's latency and turns an experiment into an outage.

Then I compare disagreements rather than aggregates, because identical totals can hide one system being better on one category and worse on another — and those sampled disagreements are the best new cases for the evaluation set.
